topic: Peninsular Plateau and Plains of Geography
description: The Northern Plains and the Peninsular Plateau are fundamental physiographic divisions of India. The Peninsular Plateau is the oldest landmass (part of the ancient Gondwanaland), while the Northern Plains are the youngest, formed by the continuous alluvial deposits brought down by Himalayan rivers.

sections.title: Geomorphological Features of the Northern Plains
sections.description: The classification of the Northern Plains based on variations in relief features and alluvial deposits.

key_concepts.explanation: A narrow belt (8-16 km wide) running parallel to the slopes of the Shiwaliks where Himalayan rivers deposit pebbles and often disappear. It is highly porous and unsuitable for agriculture.
A wet, swampy, and marshy region lying south of the Bhabar belt where underground streams re-emerge to the surface. It is traditionally characterized by dense forests and rich wildlife.

The largest part of the northern plain formed of older alluvium. It lies above the flood plains of the rivers and presents a terrace-like feature. It contains calcareous deposits locally known as 'Kankar'.
The newer, younger deposits of the flood plains. They are renewed almost every year by river floods, making them highly fertile and ideal for intensive agriculture.

sections.title: Regional Division of the Northern Plains
sections.description: Broadly divided into three sections based on the major river systems that formed them.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Formed by the Indus river and its tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej).
geographical_data.key_characteristics: A major portion of this plain lies in Pakistan. This section is heavily dominated by 'Doabs' (highly fertile land between two converging rivers).

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Extends between the Ghaggar and Teesta rivers.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: It is the largest plain covering North Indian states including Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, partly Jharkhand, and West Bengal.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Lies mostly in the state of Assam.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Formed by the Brahmaputra river and its tributaries, it is renowned for the presence of numerous riverine islands and sand bars.

important_facts.fact: Majuli, located in the Brahmaputra River in Assam, is recognized as the largest inhabited riverine island in the world.

sections.title: The Peninsular Plateau
sections.description: A tableland composed of old crystalline, igneous, and metamorphic rocks, formed by the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana landmass.

key_concepts.explanation: The part of the Peninsular plateau lying to the north of the Narmada river, covering a major area of the Malwa plateau. The Vindhyan range bounds it on the south and the Aravalis on the northwest.
A triangular landmass that lies to the south of the river Narmada. The Satpura range flanks its broad base in the north, while the Mahadev, Kaimur hills, and Maikal range form its eastern extensions.
The northeastern extension of the Peninsular plateau, drained by the Damodar river. It is extraordinarily rich in mineral resources (coal, iron ore) and is often called the 'Ruhr of India'.
The western part of the Peninsular plateau characterized by black soil of volcanic origin. The basaltic igneous rocks have denuded over time to form soil ideal for cotton cultivation.

sections.title: Western and Eastern Ghats
sections.description: The mountain ranges that mark the western and eastern edges of the Deccan Plateau respectively.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Run parallel to the western coast of India facing the Arabian Sea.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: They are continuous and can be crossed only through passes (Thal, Bhor, and Pal Ghats). Their average elevation is higher (900-1600m) and increases from north to south.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Run parallel to the eastern coast facing the Bay of Bengal, stretching from the Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: They are discontinuous, irregular, and heavily dissected by major rivers draining into the Bay of Bengal (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery).

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Located at the tri-junction of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: This mountainous region acts as the geographical meeting point where the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats converge.

important_facts.fact: Anaimudi (2695 meters) in the Annamalai hills of Kerala is the highest peak of the Western Ghats as well as the entire Peninsular Plateau.
Mahendragiri (1501 meters) in Odisha is one of the most prominent and highest peaks of the Eastern Ghats.

sections.title: Coastal Plains
sections.description: The narrow coastal strips flanking the Peninsular Plateau, running along the Arabian Sea on the west and the Bay of Bengal on the east.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: A narrow plain sandwiched between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: It consists of three sections: the Konkan coast in the north (Mumbai-Goa), the Kannad plain in the central stretch, and the Malabar coast in the south (Kerala).

geographical_data.location_or_origin: A wide, level plain lying between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal.
geographical_data.key_characteristics: It is divided into the Northern Circars (northern part) and the Coromandel Coast (southern part). Major rivers form extensive and fertile deltas here.

important_facts.fact: The Malabar Coast is famous for its 'Kayals' (backwaters), which are shallow lagoons used for fishing, inland navigation, and tourism.
Vembanad Lake in Kerala is the longest lake in India and a defining feature of the Malabar coastal plain.
Chilika Lake in Odisha, located south of the Mahanadi delta along the eastern coast, is the largest saltwater lake in India.
